title: Proof-of-Review Receipts for AI-Using Professionals
one_liner: A tamper-evident record that a named, licensed human actually reviewed AI output, backed by planted-error vigilance tests, sold to firms and their malpractice carriers.
customer: Mid-size law firms, accounting firms and physician groups using AI drafting or scribes, and the malpractice and E&O carriers, MGAs and brokers underwriting AI use.
problem: Courts worldwide have issued about 1,490 decisions on AI-hallucinated filings (1,000+ in the US by May 2026), with sanctions up to $110k and the first suspensions. More than 60% of carriers now ask about AI use in underwriting, and some add AI endorsements or exclusions. Firms cannot prove that attorney review happened beyond a policy memo.
solution: A review layer (Word and Outlook add-in, EHR plug-in, browser extension) that logs what the AI produced, what the human changed, dwell time, automated cite-check results and sign-off. It also seeds a random slice of reviews with canary errors (a fake citation, a wrong dose in a test document) to measure whether reviewers really catch them. A signed monthly review-integrity report goes to the carrier for premium credit or endorsement eligibility.
why_now: AI-hallucination sanctions are growing by about eight cases a day. The EPIC 2026 claims survey shows carriers seeing more AI-related claims, and carriers are rewriting applications and endorsements now.
revenue_model: $30-80 per professional per month, carrier and broker partnerships (revenue share on premium credits), and a cite-check add-on.
non_obvious_insight: The weak link is automation complacency, not just model hallucination. You can measure complacency the way airports measure screener vigilance, by planting known-bad items. Insurers will pay for measured human vigilance because it is a rating factor.
first_30_days: Partner with one legal-malpractice MGA or broker and 10 small firms (5-50 lawyers) through state-bar CLE channels. Ship a Word add-in that logs review and checks citations. Pilot canary errors with written consent.

title: Native-Language Translation Earpieces for Dementia Care
one_liner: Dementia-tuned real-time speech translation and a life-story phrasebook so aides can soothe residents in the language they reverted to.
customer: Memory-care communities and nursing homes with multilingual residents, and home-care agencies in NYC, Miami, LA, the Bay Area and Houston.
problem: People with dementia often revert to a first language, while 30% of care workers (60% in New York) are immigrants who speak other languages. The mismatch causes agitation, missed pain, more antipsychotic use and hospital transfers. Compliance-grade phone interpreters are too slow for a 3 am redirect.
solution: An earbud and tablet kit with speech-to-speech translation tuned for dementia (short, slow, warm, repetitive), a preloaded ADL and redirection phrasebook, resident life-story cards in their language (hometown, family, songs), and a video human-interpreter fallback within 30 seconds. Staff dashboards report agitation and PRN antipsychotic use.
why_now: Real-time on-device speech translation reached mainstream earbuds and phones in 2025-26, while visa and TPS shocks are replacing staff with workers who share fewer languages with residents.
revenue_model: $30-60 per resident per month, or $99 per aide per month, plus an implementation fee.
non_obvious_insight: Language access is treated as a compliance checkbox, not a clinical tool. Generic translation isn't tuned to dementia speech and emotion, and the measurable outcome (fewer PRN antipsychotics) is a metric operators already care about.
first_30_days: Identify five memory-care communities with Spanish-, Russian- or Chinese-speaking residents. Run $500 pilots with tablets and an interpreter fallback, and measure PRN antipsychotic use before and after.

title: Shelf Zero: Unclaimed Cremains Clearance Service
one_liner: A done-for-you compliance service that legally and respectfully empties the closet of unclaimed ashes that nearly every funeral home and crematory is afraid to touch.
customer: Independent funeral homes and crematories, where the owner or office manager pays per container. Secondary buyers are county public administrators and medical examiner offices. A third group is owners preparing to sell, whose buyers will flag the shelf in diligence.
problem: Cremation is now the majority disposition and still climbing. Families ghost after the cremation: an unpaid balance, an estrangement, a move, or a death of the only relative. State law on unclaimed remains varies widely. Search results show, for example, 120 days after written notice in Minnesota, at least 121 days in Texas, 60 days in Ohio and Nebraska, and 90 days with cemetery-contract rules in California. Directors won't scatter anything without a bulletproof paper trail, because one angry cousin surfacing four years later is a lawsuit or a board complaint. So the boxes pile up. A two-generation-old home can have dozens or hundreds, and staff feel guilt every time they walk past the shelf.
solution: A per-state playbook run as a service. Intake is a spreadsheet upload of name, date, contract and contact. Then skip-tracing for next of kin and authorizing agents, certified-mail and email notices on the statutory timeline, and a timestamped evidence file. Lawful disposition follows, through partner columbarium common niches, scattering gardens or sea scattering, each with a signed Certificate of Lawful Disposition per box. Veterans are identified through records requests and routed to the free national-cemetery inurnment route and Missing in America Project-type volunteers. Families who surface late can still reclaim through the funeral home for a small fee. An ongoing alert that flags containers at day 30, 60 and 90 stops the shelf refilling.
why_now: Cremation share keeps rising and household budgets are stretched, so abandonment is increasing. Consolidators such as SCI keep buying independents (about 22 funeral homes and 2 cemeteries for roughly $101M in 2025 per its filings). Their diligence treats an uncleared shelf as a liability, so retiring third-generation owners suddenly need a clean inventory. Skip-tracing and document automation are now cheap enough to run per box at a profit.
revenue_model: $175-$400 per container, tiered by state notice complexity. A $1,500-$3,000 pre-sale shelf audit and clearance bundle sells to owners about to list. A $49-$99/month ongoing aging-alert subscription covers new cases. Disposition partner fees (niche, scattering, transport) are passed through with a margin.
non_obvious_insight: The problem isn't the ashes, it's the paper trail. Nobody wants to be the person who scattered too early, so the shelf grows for decades. Outsiders assume it's a handful of boxes and a sad footnote. Inside, it's a compounding legal and emotional liability that every owner would pay a flat fee to make disappear, and the product being sold is really indemnifying documentation plus dignity, not disposal logistics.
first_30_days: Pick Ohio, Minnesota and Texas, where statutory safe harbors are clearest. Pay a funeral-law attorney a few thousand dollars to draft the three state notice templates and the disposition certificate. Offer a free 'shelf audit' to 30 homes via the state funeral directors' association newsletter and the private director Facebook groups. Convert five homes at $250 per box as pilots. Sign one local columbarium or church for a common-niche arrangement and one veterans-remains volunteer chapter.

title: Thermal Safety Certification for Recovery Studios
one_liner: Staff certification, medication-aware intake screening and water-quality logging that insurers will soon require of sauna and cold-plunge operators.
customer: Contrast-therapy studios, gym recovery rooms, hotels and spas, paying monthly per location.
problem: Chain: studios are rolling out at speed (one brand added 25 locations in about 20 months and plans 100 more), so hundreds of new hires with no clinical training run 190F rooms and shared 40F tubs; customers increasingly take GLP-1s, blood-pressure meds or diuretics that raise fainting and dehydration risk; shared plunge water has no consistent standard and health departments are unsure how to classify it. One serious incident will trigger insurer exclusions and regulator attention.
solution: Three-part kit: a 90-minute 'Thermal Host' certification with annual refresh; tablet check-in screening (conditions and medications mapped to green/yellow/red session guidance plus waiver logging); and a water sensor pack (ORP, pH, chlorine, temperature) that auto-generates logs for inspectors and insurers.
why_now: The recovery boom (Nordic-style attendance up about 33 percent in 2025), mass GLP-1 use (about 1 in 8 adults), and no existing standard mean insurers and health departments are about to look for controls.
revenue_model: $99-199 per month per location, $39 per staff certification, sensor rental $49 per month per tub, plus insurer or broker referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: Be the standard before the incident: insurers would rather subsidize a certification than write exclusions, and the screening data is a wedge to premium programs. GLP-1 plus heat is the specific collision no one is training for.
first_30_days: Draft the protocol with a sports-medicine physician and a pool-operations consultant, sell it to 5 independent studios in one metro at a discounted founding rate, and ask two studio-focused insurance brokers for a premium credit for certified locations.

title: The Unrecorded Room
one_liner: Hourly, certified no-recording rooms (phone lockers, no AI notetakers, analog paper only) for conversations too candid to survive a transcript.
customer: General counsels and outside counsel, boards and special committees, M&A and restructuring teams, VC-founder negotiations, HR investigators, and labor-management negotiators in one dense business district. They pay $200-400/hour or $2-5k/month firm memberships.
problem: AI notetakers now sit in most meetings. In mid-2026 firms such as Mayer Brown were warning that they create discoverable transcripts and privilege risk, and in February 2026 Judge Rakoff (SDNY) held that a defendant's chats with an AI platform were not privileged. Virtual meetings can't be sealed. Even offices are full of transcribing laptops, smart speakers, and phones. Leaders' workaround is 'let's take a walk'.
solution: Rooms with phone and laptop lockers, RF-shielded walls, whiteboards and paper pads, and a sign-in ritual. All attendees sign an 'Unrecorded' attestation that no recording or AI tool is in use. The venue logs who attended, never what was said. It offers concierge booking and a 'war room' day package. Counsel reviews the model so the room never destroys existing records, only avoids creating new ones. Later it certifies hotel suites and law-firm floors as 'Unrecorded Certified'.
why_now: AI notetaker penetration is high, and 2026 legal commentary and case law make the privilege and discovery risk concrete. The person paying is the person personally liable for the record.
revenue_model: Hourly room fees, firm memberships, and day-long war-room packages ($3k). White-label and certification fees from hotels and law-firm floors.
non_obvious_insight: In a fully transcribed world, the provable absence of a record is a premium product, and the buyer is the person with legal liability. Invitation to the unrecorded room becomes a high-trust status marker. It is a venue business that is not competing with coworking, because it sells evidence that nothing was kept.
first_30_days: Lease 3-4 rooms inside an existing coworking or law-office building on revenue share. Give CLE talks at the local bar association on 'AI notetakers and privilege' as a cheap lead engine. Have a TSCM consultant validate a low-cost shielding and locker setup. Pre-sell 10 firm memberships.

title: Dealer-Fee Decoder for Solar and Home Loans
one_liner: Use the auto F&I trick of hiding the buy-down in the price to expose the hidden 'dealer fee' inside 0% and low-rate solar, HVAC and roofing loans, then sell the evidence to consumer lawyers and the refinance to credit unions.
customer: First: consumer-protection and TILA law firms and legal aid running home-improvement and solar loan cases, at $49 to $149 per decoded loan. Second: credit unions and community banks that pay $150 to $300 per funded takeout loan.
problem: A '0% for 12 months' or '2.99% for 20 years' home-improvement loan is not cheap. The lender charges the contractor a discount or 'dealer fee' that commonly runs into double digits on promotional-rate loans, and the contractor recovers it by inflating the price for financed customers. It's the same mechanic as a dealer's reserve and buy-down in an auto F&I office. The borrower sees a low APR, cannot see the cash price they should have been quoted, and often pays a financed price 15 to 30% above the cash price. Minnesota's attorney general has sued GoodLeap over hidden fees folded into loan amounts, and complaints keep growing. Homeowners left with orphaned systems and no tax credit are a sympathetic and litigable group.
solution: A document-parsing decoder. The homeowner or lawyer uploads the contract, TILA disclosure and any competing cash quote. The tool extracts price, APR, term and any disclosed fee, and estimates the implied cash price and implied finance charge, meaning how much of the price is really interest. It compares this to a regional cash-price benchmark built from scraped quotes, contractor bid sites and permit data. It outputs a plain-language one-pager and a lawyer-grade exhibit for TILA and UDAP claims, then offers a credit-union takeout quote for the true payoff amount.
why_now: The federal residential solar tax credit for homeowner purchases ended after 2025, a wave of installers went bankrupt and left homeowners with loans on systems nobody services, state attorneys general have started suing, and the CFPB's federal enforcement has faded so states and private plaintiffs are the enforcement. Contingency-fee plaintiff firms are already advertising for GoodLeap-type cases and need faster intake screening.
revenue_model: Per-case fee from law firms ($49 to $149), a subscription for high-volume firms ($499 per month), and a bounty from credit unions for each funded refinance or takeout loan. Later, a compliance benchmark sold to honest contractors, to lenders and to regulators.
non_obvious_insight: Consumer advocates attack solar lenders as if the fee were unique to solar. A finance manager knows it is standard structure anywhere a merchant can 'buy down' a rate: the retail price quietly carries the cost. What law firms lack is not the theory but cheap, defensible, per-loan numbers to screen thousands of leads. The cash price counterfactual is the missing piece and the F&I mindset is exactly what tells you where to look for it.
first_30_days: Collect 200 real solar and HVAC loan document sets and cash-vs-financed quote pairs from public complaints, forums and two or three law-firm partners. Build the parser and implied-price model on them. Offer three plaintiff firms with active solar-loan intake 25 free screens each, then charge $99 a case. Meet two credit unions with home-improvement loan programs to agree a bounty for takeouts.

title: Whey-Free Calf Milk Replacer
one_liner: Sell alternative-protein milk replacer to calf raisers hit by whey prices, where functionality demands are far looser than in food.
customer: Calf ranches, dairy heifer raisers, beef-on-dairy operations and regional feed mills.
problem: Calf milk replacers lean on whey protein, whose price is up 108% in two years, squeezing the operations that supply beef-on-dairy calves at the moment the herd is at a 75-year low.
solution: A milk replacer built on potato, pea, hydrolyzed and fermentation-derived proteins plus a tuned fat blend, with growth-trial performance guarantees.
why_now: Whey has become scarcer than the cheese it came from, and record calf values make feed cost per pound of gain a live issue.
revenue_model: Bag sales per pound plus per-head feeding programs with performance guarantees.
non_obvious_insight: Sell alternative proteins to animals first: feed has no clear-drink functionality bar and the buyer measures ROI in daily gain rather than taste.
first_30_days: Hire a ruminant nutritionist, run a feeding trial at two calf ranches, and offer pilot programs priced per pound of gain.

title: Tip Provenance Ledger for Tipped-Occupation Employers
one_liner: An evidence trail that classifies every dollar as a voluntary tip, service charge, pool or cash tip, to support new tip-deduction reporting.
customer: Restaurants, bars, salons, spas, barbershops, valet operators, car washes and delivery fleets with 5-60 workers on Toast, Square, Clover or spreadsheets, and self-employed booth renters in tipped occupations.
problem: The 2025 reconciliation law made qualified tips and overtime deductible, and the IRS says employers must file information returns on them. Workers now have an incentive to relabel pay as tips. Owners must separate voluntary tips from mandatory service charges, pooled tips and cash tips, and errors trigger worker disputes and IRS letters.
solution: Ingest POS, payment and payroll data and tag each dollar with provenance. Produce the W-2 or 1099 support schedule, worker-facing statements so employees can claim their deduction, and an audit binder. Flag anomalies such as a service charge quietly recategorized as tips at year-end.
why_now: Tax year 2026 is the first full year under the new rules and W-2s are due January 31, 2027. Payroll vendors are adding fields but not provenance.
revenue_model: $29-79 per location per month, plus $3 per worker statement. Channel through POS app stores and restaurant bookkeepers.
non_obvious_insight: A deduction that is valuable to both worker and owner creates an incentive to reclassify, which makes the evidence trail the product, in the same way that exemption certificates support sales-tax deductions. Payroll vendors will add a field but not the audit trail.
first_30_days: Recruit 15 restaurants and salons through bookkeepers. Build a Square and Toast CSV importer and offer a free Q4 tip audit. Convert audit customers to an annual plan ahead of the W-2 deadline.

title: Bulk Records-Request Refinery, Septic-First
one_liner: Build datasets that do not exist by filing thousands of automated public-records requests to county health departments, then reading the scans with vision models and selling address-level reports.
customer: Home inspectors, buyer's agents, title and closing attorneys, and mortgage lenders and insurers in septic- and well-heavy markets, who pay per address report or a monthly subscription. Later customers are insurers and lenders buying bulk address-level datasets.
problem: About one in five US homes runs on septic and millions rely on private wells. Permits, inspections, pump-outs, repair and abandonment records sit in more than 3,000 county and town health departments, in paper, scans and idiosyncratic portals. There is no national database. Buyers sign blind and face 15-50k USD failed-system replacements. Inspectors and agents make phone calls to find records, or skip the check.
solution: A records-request engine. It knows each state's open-records statute, fee categories and portal type. It bulk-files requests, tracks deadlines, and follows up. A vision-language pipeline reads handwritten and scanned forms, extracts fields (install date, tank size, drainfield type, repairs, failed inspections, well depth and tests) and geocodes them to parcels. Sell address-level reports for 39-99 USD, with a guarantee of retrieve or refund at first. Every answered request becomes a permanent proprietary data asset, so the data compounds. The same engine expands to other records with no national database: hydrant flow tests, fire inspections, certificates of occupancy, unpermitted-work flags, underground tanks and radon.
why_now: Vision-language models now read messy handwriting and scanned forms at fractions of a cent per page, which made this economically impossible until recently. Most jurisdictions have moved to online request portals, making bulk filing feasible without postage and paper. Agents can draft statute-specific requests and chase deadlines automatically. Home-inspection firms are looking for differentiated services in a slow transaction market.
revenue_model: Pay-per-address report (39-99 USD), inspector subscriptions (149-399 USD per month for unlimited lookups in their region), and enterprise data licenses to insurers and lenders. Later, sell the engine as a service to other data-hungry industries that need one specific municipal record type at national scale.
non_obvious_insight: Government data is not secret, just expensive to collect, and that friction is the moat. Every request is legal, cheap and repeatable, but nobody wants to make 3,000 of them by hand, so once you have, nobody can scrape or replicate your dataset from the web. Concierge fulfillment lets you get paid on day one before the automation exists, and every manual retrieval trains the pipeline.
first_30_days: Choose one state with a septic-heavy housing stock and a friendly open-records law (for example, a state where county health departments handle onsite wastewater, such as North Carolina). Check the state law for commercial-requester restrictions and fee schedules. Offer 20 local home inspectors a 75 USD 'we retrieve the septic record or refund you' service, fulfilled manually or semi-manually at first. Simultaneously file bulk requests to every county health department for historical records. Run the vision extraction pipeline on the first few thousand pages, and use the results to pitch a subscription to inspector networks and title companies.

title: Orphan Lien Clearance Desk for Title Agents
one_liner: A flat-fee curative service that proves dead solar fixture filings and other zombie liens are dead (or gets them released) so home closings stop stalling.
customer: Independent title and escrow agencies and real estate attorneys in high-solar states (AZ, CA, FL, TX, NJ, NC, NV, CO), billed per file and usually paid by the seller at closing. Listing agents in solar-heavy markets are a second channel.
problem: Sunnova filed Chapter 11 in June 2025 (500,000+ customers), Mosaic and PosiGen followed, and the residential solar credit ended for 2026 installs, so thousands of homes carry UCC-1 fixture filings and recorded solar-lease notices held by dead, merged or reassigned entities. Title examiners flag every one. Agents can't tell who holds the debt now, whether the filing is even still legally effective, or how to get a termination, so closings slip days or weeks. The people currently serving this are consumer SEO and lead-gen sites, not the title agents who actually need it solved on a deadline.
solution: Per-file lien autopsy delivered in 48 hours. (1) Pull the recorded instrument and any continuation or termination filings from the county index and the Secretary of State. (2) Compute lapse under UCC 9-515 (five years unless continued in the six-month window). (3) Trace the assignment and servicer chain through bankruptcy dockets and servicer notices. (4) Deliver either an underwriter-ready 'lapsed, no exception' memo, or a payoff/estoppel request plus a pre-drafted termination (UCC-3, or debtor-filed termination where the statute allows) recorded in that county's required format. Recorded memoranda of lease, which do not lapse, get a release workflow instead. Later expand the same engine to satisfied-but-never-released mortgages, expired judgment liens, dead PACE liens and resurfaced zombie second mortgages.
why_now: 2025-2026 solar installer bankruptcies (Sunnova, Mosaic, PosiGen) and the end of the residential solar credit produced the largest single wave of orphaned fixture filings ever recorded. 2018-2021 installs are now hitting their five-year lapse dates just as those homes come to market. Title agents are short-staffed and want to outsource curative work, and an LLM can read county index entries and bankruptcy docket text cheaply.
revenue_model: Flat fee of about $395-$900 per cleared file, contingent on clear-to-close. Agencies with volume pay $299/month plus a reduced per-file rate. White-label API for underwriters and closing software later.
non_obvious_insight: Half the 'problem liens' in solar-heavy counties are already legally dead, but the county index never shows lapse, so examiners treat a 2019 fixture filing as live forever. Clerks watch continuation filings come in, and most small installers never filed one. The work is proof of death, not payoff. Insiders also know the recorded 'notice of lease' is a different animal that never lapses, and that a clerk must record a debtor-filed termination on its face, since the office is ministerial.
first_30_days: Offer the first five files free to 3-5 independent title agencies in Phoenix, Tampa and Sacramento. Build the lapse calculator and county-index lookups for about 10 counties. Get one regional agent underwriter to accept a standard lapse-memo format. Then price at $495 per file and ask each agency for a testimonial and two referrals to listing agents.

title: Posthumous Likeness Trusts for Creators
one_liner: Estate planning for people whose face and voice already earn money: who may license their AI replica, who may not, and how it is enforced.
customer: Mid-tier creators (100K-5M followers), podcasters, voice actors, and the small managers and MCNs who represent them.
problem: Consumer-grade video and voice cloning means anyone's likeness can be recreated after death. Laws are a patchwork (Tennessee's ELVIS Act and California's 2024 digital-replica laws, a federal NO FAKES bill pending). Creators' estates hold real income (channels, catalogs, sponsorships) but have no instrument to permit, forbid or license replicas. Platforms handle it ad hoc.
solution: A 'Likeness Trust Kit': (1) a will or trust addendum with a digital-replica directive (allowed uses, revenue splits, ban list, who decides), (2) a registry and notice system aimed at platforms and AI vendors, (3) monitoring for unauthorized replicas and template takedowns, (4) a channel-continuity plan (access, memorialization, pinned messages), and (5) an optional licensing desk for approved 'legacy' uses.
why_now: The fall-2025 backlash over AI videos of deceased public figures made estates' concerns public. State post-mortem publicity laws changed in 2024, and platforms have begun shipping likeness-detection tools for creators (verify current status). No estate product has priced in that a voice and face are now licensable and misusable assets.
revenue_model: $1,500-$3,500 setup for documents and registry, $19-$79/month monitoring, and 10-20% of licensed uses. Managers buy in bulk.
non_obvious_insight: Estate lawyers treat likeness as a celebrity issue. The willing buyers are working creators who already understand platforms and already earn from their persona, and they are numerous and reachable through managers.
first_30_days: Partner with an entertainment attorney. Draft a template addendum. Sell to 10 creator managers at about $2K per client. Use off-the-shelf detection tools for monitoring and publish a public 'creator death checklist' for lead generation.

title: Guardrail Gateway for Hotel AI Agents
one_liner: A proxy between hotel AI agents (voice, chat, booking) and PMS, POS and door-lock APIs that enforces per-action permissions, spend limits and human approval for irreversible actions.
customer: Hotel AI vendors that need enterprise trust, hotel groups' IT and security teams, and cyber insurers.
problem: Hotels are deploying agents fast (Dextr AI raised a USD 6.7M seed for hotel voice agents on 24 Sep 2026, and 109 AI use cases have been catalogued across 39 hotel systems). Practitioner commentary warns agents often hold API access built for trusted staff, so a prompt-injected guest message could trigger refunds, comps, rate changes or key issuance. PMS platforms have no concept of a scoped agent identity.
solution: An API and MCP gateway in front of PMS platforms (start with one that has a public API). It is read-only by default, applies caps on write actions (small refunds auto-approve, larger ones go to staff for approval in Slack or WhatsApp), redacts personal data, has a kill switch and keeps immutable logs. It ships with a red-team pack of injection attacks.
why_now: Agents are moving from pilots to production in 2026, PMS vendors are opening APIs, and agent protocols such as MCP are mainstream. Insurers and enterprise buyers are starting to ask for controls.
revenue_model: USD 49-149 per property per month, OEM licences to AI vendors, and insurer referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: In the agent gold rush the scarce item is the permission model, not the agent. AI vendors will pay for it as a sales enabler, and insurers will pay because it caps their loss.
first_30_days: Build against one PMS with a public API (Mews or Cloudbeds). Sign 2 hotel AI startups as design partners, and publish a red-team report showing injection weaknesses in demo agents (with permission) to earn press and inbound interest.

title: Sell Heat Pumps to Health Plans
one_liner: Sell home electrification to Medicaid and Medicare Advantage plans as a cost-of-care reduction instead of selling it to homeowners as a climate upgrade.
customer: Medicaid managed-care organizations, Medicare Advantage plans (supplemental benefits) and nonprofit hospital community-benefit budgets. They pay per completed install, plus an outcome bonus.
problem: The 25C credit ended 12/31/2025, homeowners face ~$9,000 heat pump quotes, and HEAR rebates roll out unevenly by state. Meanwhile health plans pay for asthma and COPD ER visits, heat illness and gas-stove-related respiratory events that cost thousands per admission.
solution: A 'clinical electrification program in a box'. Claims data finds members with asthma, COPD or heat vulnerability. A vetted contractor network installs a heat pump, heat pump water heater or induction cooktop. The program stacks HEAR/HOMES rebates so the plan pays only the gap, tracks ER visits and medication use, and reports ROI to the plan. Billing runs through Medicaid health-related-social-needs and in-lieu-of-service pathways or MA supplemental benefits.
why_now: Some state Medicaid waivers (Oregon's climate-device benefit) and MA plans already pay for air conditioners and air filtration. $8.8B of HEAR/HOMES money needs matching demand. Federal homeowner credits are gone, so the old buyer has weakened.
revenue_model: $2-6k net per install paid by the plan after rebate stacking, a platform fee, contractor take-rate, and outcome-based bonuses.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders keep trying to improve the homeowner's payback. The payer with the fastest ROI is the one who pays for ambulances. Health plans have budget lines, claims data to find the right homes, and no need for a 10-year payback.
first_30_days: Pick one state with a Medicaid climate-device benefit or a Southwest MA plan. Find two MCO community-health leads. Build claims-based targeting analytics. Run a 25-home pilot with one contractor using existing HEAR or utility rebates, and write a one-page ROI memo from baseline ER usage.

title: AI Re-Post Radar with First-Publication Proof
one_liner: A seal-then-watch tool that timestamps a creator's work before publishing and finds AI-reworded, re-voiced copies, with a ready-to-file complaint.
customer: Educational and commentary YouTubers, podcast producers and paid-newsletter writers with 10k-500k audiences, and small MCNs that manage them.
problem: The industry argues about whether a piece is AI-made. For a creator being ripped off, the deciding fact is who published first. Faceless channels can transcribe, reword and re-voice a human video or post within hours. YouTube's Jul 16 policy on generic or repetitive content helps in principle, but enforcement depends on complaints, and long-tail creators lack Content ID-style tooling.
solution: A pre-publish 'seal' takes a hash of script, audio and footage plus an embedding of the transcript, anchored to a public timestamp log. A radar then checks YouTube, TikTok, Substack, Medium, RSS and podcast directories for semantic near-duplicates, using transcript embeddings so reworded copies still match. It scores them, and drafts a YouTube reused-content complaint, DMCA notice or EU DSA notice with the timestamp proof attached.
why_now: Rewriting and re-voicing are now nearly free, while platforms have just adopted policies that penalize repetitive content but rely on rights-holders to report. Embeddings make cheap semantic matching practical.
revenue_model: $29-99/month per creator, $5 per auto-filed takedown bundle, and agency plans for MCNs.
non_obvious_insight: Origin time beats origin type. A timestamped record survives rewording, re-encoding and watermark stripping, while 'made by AI or not' is a probabilistic argument. The evidence is the product.
first_30_days: Build a transcript-and-embedding pipeline on the YouTube Data API and Whisper, limited to each customer's niche keywords. Recruit 10 creators from YouTuber Discords and demo by finding real re-posts of their videos within the first hour. Charge $29/month after the free scan.

title: Government Property Control Kit for New Defense Makers
one_liner: A fixed-price property-system-in-a-box (tags, procedures, mock audit, reconciliation) that keeps first-time defense manufacturers from failing their government property audit and having payments withheld.
customer: New-entrant defense manufacturers (drone, munitions second-source and component startups) and small machine shops that receive government-furnished property, plus primes that flow the property clauses down and want their subs certified.
problem: Contractors holding government-furnished property must run a property management system with receiving reports, physical inventory, loss and damage reporting, and reconciliation to the contract's property list. If the government disapproves the system, contracting officers can direct payment withholds. Small shops run this on spreadsheets and no one is the accountable hand-receipt holder. Property administrators cannot coach, and consultants bill $200-400 an hour.
solution: A packaged offering. A one-day on-site 'mock property system analysis' run by former property administrators. Asset tagging and mobile scanning. Templated procedures, forms and a monthly reconciliation to the contract property list. Audit-ready binder and annual physical inventory support. Ongoing loss/damage/destruction reporting and excess-property disposition paperwork. Position it to program managers, not compliance officers, as schedule protection.
why_now: The Revolutionary FAR Overhaul rewrote Part 45 (Government Property), with model deviation text implemented from November 2025, so many contractors are rereading their obligations. Defense spending and drone and munitions ramp-ups are pulling venture-backed hardware companies and first-time subs into contracts with government-furnished property. CMMC phase-ins compete for the same small compliance budgets, so property control gets ignored until an audit finds it.
revenue_model: Mock audit at $6-15k, then $500-2,000 a month for software plus fractional property-officer support, plus per-asset tagging fees. Prime-sponsored programs where a prime pays to certify its sub base.
non_obvious_insight: The property system is about 90% behavior and 10% software: who signs for what, and whether there is an unbroken trail from receipt to disposition. Auditors find the same handful of deficiencies again and again (no receiving report, no physical inventory, no reconciliation, no loss report), so a checklist-driven fixed-price service works better than custom consulting. The strongest sponsor is the prime, because a sub's disapproved system threatens the prime's own schedule and cash.
first_30_days: Pull first-time awardees from SBIR/STTR winners and public contract awards that carry government-furnished property. Offer 10 of them a $2,500 one-day GFP health check. Publish a one-page 'seven findings auditors keep writing' as lead magnet. Partner with a regional APEX Accelerator for referrals and a CMMC registered provider organization for cross-sell. Turn the first 3 engagements into a templated binder and a simple scanning workflow before building any software.

title: Hype-Item Triage for Thrift and Charity Shops
one_liner: A 10-second back-room scan station that tells thrift and charity staff which donated sneakers and collectibles are worth $150 instead of $12, then lists them online for a revenue share.
customer: Independent Goodwill regionals, church and charity thrift shops, Plato's Closet-style franchisees, consignment shops and estate-sale companies. They pay a rev share on the uplift, or $199 per month per store.
problem: Thrift pricers are paid to move volume and price shoes at a flat $8 to $25 by category. Meanwhile teen and adult resellers ('pickers') walk the racks right after restock and buy the $12 pairs worth $200 and up. Donations are the shop's raw material, and the shop is giving the profit to the pickers. Charities lose real money, and staff cannot read a style code or tell a real pair from a fake, so they either underprice or avoid the risk.
solution: A tablet at the sorting table. Staff photograph the tongue tag or box label. OCR pulls the style code and size, then the app returns resale value, days-to-sell, condition-adjusted price and known fake tells for that model. Anything over $60 goes into an 'online' bin. Our remote team of college and teen resellers lists, ships and remits the shop's share, so the shop needs no e-commerce staff. Later categories: trading cards, LEGO, vintage tees, Stanley cups, Pokemon sealed product, watches.
why_now: Thrift has boomed with Gen Z while tariffs push shoppers to secondhand, which also means more pickers hitting the same racks. Multimodal models now read tag photos accurately and cheaply. Donations arrive in volume, but shop margins are squeezed by picker competition and labor costs. Charities have never had a hype-specific tool.
revenue_model: 20% to 30% of net sale price on items routed to online, or a SaaS fee per store. Charities are motivated because it is found money for their programs.
non_obvious_insight: The biggest sneaker sourcing channel for resellers is a flat-price system that cannot see value. The knowledge needed is tiny: style code, size, box, one authenticity tell. That is why resellers win, and it can be sold to the seller side. Being reseller-native gives me trust with staff and the sourcing instincts to know which categories are next.
first_30_days: Offer three local charity thrift shops a free two-week pilot. I sort through their back room on a Saturday, list the top 30 items, and split proceeds with the charity (charity 70%, us 30%). Track the uplift versus what those items would have sold for on the floor. Turn the numbers into a one-page case study and pitch 20 more independent thrift operators.

title: Grid-Code Models for AI Data Centers
one_liner: Validated dynamic load models and ride-through test packages so data centers can pass the same grid-code exams that generators pass.
customer: Interconnection teams at hyperscalers, neoclouds and colo developers, and their EPCs. Transmission owners and ISOs need the models validated, and the developer pays.
problem: About 1.5 GW of Northern Virginia data center load tripped offline together during a 2024 fault. AI training loads swing tens of MW in seconds, and xAI buys Megapacks largely to smooth them. Texas SB 6 and NERC large-load work now push for ride-through and dynamic models, but no standard model library or test lab exists for GPU cluster, power-supply and UPS stacks.
solution: Build a parametric EMT and PSS/E model library for common facility architectures (UPS topologies, PSU behavior, 800V DC). Validate it with hardware-in-the-loop tests at a partner lab. Sell per-project model packages, ride-through study reports and compliance-ready certification letters. Charge a subscription to keep models current as hardware changes.
why_now: Multi-GW campuses, NERC's large-load task force and Texas and PJM interconnection rules in 2025-26 are turning load models from optional into a gating item.
revenue_model: $75-300k per project for the model and study, an annual model-maintenance subscription, and test or certification fees paid by UPS and power-shelf OEMs.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone frames data centers as demand. The grid now treats them as a dynamic device, like a giant inverter-based generator. Inverter-generator modeling became a consulting industry after events like the 2016 Blue Cut fire, and large-load modeling will follow. The model library is the moat.
first_30_days: Recruit one or two power-electronics engineers from a utility or ISO. Publish an open primer on GPU-load oscillation. Contact interconnection leads at 10 neoclouds and 5 TO planners. Sell a $15k 'large-load model gap analysis'. Sign a university hardware-in-the-loop lab as a partner.

title: Memory Budget CI for Game Studios
one_liner: CI tooling and fixed-fee audits that enforce RAM and VRAM budgets per target device, because the assumption that hardware gets better each generation just broke.
customer: Mid-size PC and console studios (30-300 staff) shipping in 2027 to Steam Deck, Switch 2 and 8-16GB PCs.
problem: AI data centers are absorbing the RAM supply. Valve's Steam Machine launched at $1,049 against an early target of about $800, Xbox prices rose, and Switch 2 goes to $499.99 on 2026-09-01. The installed base will stay at today's memory ceilings for years, but studios budget memory as a fixed cap and find regressions in late QA.
solution: An Unreal, Unity and Godot CI plugin that builds against device memory profiles, snapshots per-level memory, attributes growth to specific assets and pull requests, and suggests fixes (texture format changes, streaming pool sizes, audio bank downsampling). Sold alongside a 3-week 'memory diet' audit that finds duplicated and unstripped assets.
why_now: Memory vendors now quote a monthly price and a yes-or-no on volume, per a Valve engineer. Console and handheld price hikes in 2026 mean players will not upgrade into new game requirements. Studios are planning holiday 2026-27 lineups now.
revenue_model: $15-40k per audit, $400-2,500 per month per studio for CI, and later a subscription to a device-profile and min-spec benchmark database.
non_obvious_insight: The industry's optimization culture is about frame time. When hardware gets pricier over its life, the cheapest way to grow the addressable market is to shrink footprint, and most footprint is asset-pipeline waste that can be found and fixed automatically.
first_30_days: Publish an analysis of Steam minimum-spec trends versus the Hardware Survey to get inbound. Ship a free open-source memory snapshot diff tool for Unity and Unreal. Offer free audits to 5 studios in exchange for case studies, and convert 2 into paid engagements.

title: Neutral Noise-and-Flight Monitors for Drone Hubs
angle: Pairing 2: Logistics and physical automation x Trust and verification markets (lens: audits and reputation)
one_liner: Independent noise and flight-log monitoring that gives cities and neighbors a referee for drone-delivery hub permits, and gives operators and retail hosts approvable evidence.
customer: Drone-delivery operators and the retailers hosting hubs at store sites, paying to win and keep permits. City planning departments and neighborhood groups are the audience.
problem: Cities cannot regulate flight paths but can zone launch hubs. Northglenn requires a special-use permit, a 200 ft residential buffer and 65 dB at the property line. Wing and Walmart target 270+ sites by 2027 and Lowe's launched on Sep 28, 2026, so each site needs a hearing. Neighbors distrust operator-supplied noise data, cities lack staff and gear to check 65 dB, and a $5k-$15k consultant noise study is one-off and stale on day one.
solution: A permit-ready package. Before the application, a 7-day baseline at the property lines with calibrated low-cost acoustic sensors. After launch, continuous monitoring, tamper-evident logs, a public dashboard and alerts, matched to operator flight logs to attribute each event. An annual certification report cities can write into conditions of approval. Complaint triage: 'was a drone there at 3:14 pm? yes, 62 dB, within limit.'
why_now: The retail-scale rollout (Walmart/Wing 270+ sites, Lowe's/Wing/DoorDash launch on Sep 28, 2026, Zipline past 2M deliveries) is hitting local ground rules. Amazon paused after an Oct 2025 crane collision, so safety and trust are sensitive. Cities are drafting rules now.
revenue_model: $1,500 baseline and report per site. $300-$600/mo per site for monitoring, dashboard and certification. Optional city-charged permit fee. The city chooses the vendor, and raw data is public to protect neutrality.
non_obvious_insight: Local permitting, not the FAA, is the binding constraint on drone-delivery rollout. The currency of permits is neighbor trust, so a neutral measurement with a public dashboard is worth more than a better noise model. The party both sides accept as referee wins, and the fee is paid by whoever needs approval. Conflict-of-interest guards are the product: public raw data, no success fees, a firewall from operators.
first_30_days: Buy 10 sensors and calibrate them. Pick 3 cities with active hub hearings. Offer a free baseline for one live application at a store site. Get a city planner to reference the method in conditions of approval. Sign the first paid contract with a retail host or operator. Aim for 15-30 monitored sites by month 6.

title: FEOC and Cyber Passport for Batteries
one_liner: A serial-number-level ledger of material-assistance content and firmware and comms attestations for storage projects, built for tax-credit buyers and insurers.
customer: C&I and utility-scale storage developers and integrators, tax-credit transfer buyers (banks and insurers), and lenders.
problem: FEOC rules require 55% non-FEOC content for storage starting construction in 2026, rising to 75% by 2030. About 80% of US cells are Chinese and non-compliant projects run about 43% pricier. IRS cost tables are not due until 2027, so nobody can prove compliance. Buyers of tax credits and insurers need evidence, and concern about undocumented radios in imported inverters adds a cyber layer.
solution: A workflow and ledger that captures the bill of materials at cell and module level with supplier attestations and cost tables, then computes the material-assistance ratio conservatively. Each project gets an audit-ready evidence packet. Optional teardown, RF and firmware attestation runs through a partner lab. The 'passport' is what transfer buyers and insurers accept.
why_now: FEOC applies to 2026 construction starts, the tax-credit transfer market is doing diligence at scale, and tariffs are rising.
revenue_model: $15-50k per project, $2-5k a month SaaS per developer, verification fees from transfer buyers, and cost-plus lab attestation.
non_obvious_insight: The burden is evidence, not sourcing. With IRS guidance missing, the first firm whose conservative methodology gets accepted becomes the de facto standard, and insurers will only underwrite recapture cover against that record.
first_30_days: Publish a free MACR calculator with conservative assumptions. Interview 10 developers and three tax-credit transfer buyers. Sell three paid compliance-file builds at ~$15k for 2026-start projects. Pre-agree terms with an attestation lab.
